directAnswer: Pope Urban IV was Jacques Pantaléon, the son of a shoemaker from Troyes in France, who reigned from 29 August 1261 to 2 October 1264. He was Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem when elected, and he is best known for establishing the Feast of Corpus Christi for the whole Church in 1264.

sections.h2: From a Troyes Workshop to the Patriarchate of Jerusalem
paras: Jacques Pantaléon came from modest origins in Troyes, in the county of Champagne; medieval sources describe his father as a shoemaker. He studied in Paris and entered church service, rising through posts that included archdeacon at Liège, bishop of Verdun, and papal legate in Germany and the Baltic lands.

In 1255 Alexander IV named him Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, a see then administered from the crusader city of Acre. He had come to the papal court on business for the Holy Land when Alexander IV died in 1261. The small college of cardinals, unable to agree on one of their own after three months, chose him though he was not a cardinal.

sections.h2: Transiturus and the Feast of Corpus Christi
paras: At Liège, Jacques had known of the movement begun by St. Juliana of Cornillon, an Augustinian nun who promoted a special feast in honor of the Eucharist. The diocese of Liège adopted such a feast in the 1240s. As pope, Urban extended it to the universal Church through the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo in 1264, fixing it on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost.

Tradition holds that Urban asked Thomas Aquinas, then teaching at Orvieto where the papal court stayed, to compose the liturgical office for the feast, including hymns still sung today such as Pange lingua and its closing verses Tantum ergo. Popular tradition also connects the decree with the Eucharistic miracle reported at Bolsena in 1263, though the bull itself does not mention it. Because Urban died soon after, the feast spread slowly until it was confirmed in the early fourteenth century.

sections.h2: Charles of Anjou and the Fight over Sicily
paras: Urban inherited the conflict with Manfred, the Hohenstaufen ruler of Sicily. Abandoning the earlier English candidacy, he opened negotiations with Charles of Anjou, brother of King Louis IX of France, to take the Sicilian crown as a vassal of the Holy See. These talks laid the foundation for the Angevin conquest that his successor would complete.

He also strengthened the French presence in the curia, creating a number of French cardinals. In the East, the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII had retaken Constantinople shortly before Urban's election, ending the Latin Empire; Urban both encouraged efforts to restore it and opened contacts with Michael about church union.

sections.h2: A Pope Who Never Lived in Rome
paras: Rome's factional politics kept Urban away from the city for his entire reign. He resided chiefly at Viterbo and Orvieto, and he died at Perugia on 2 October 1264. He was buried in Perugia's cathedral. His three-year pontificate is short, but each year on Corpus Christi the Church still keeps the feast he made universal.

keyFacts: Born Jacques Pantaléon at Troyes, son of a shoemaker
Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem when elected; not a cardinal
Instituted the Feast of Corpus Christi for the universal Church with Transiturus (1264)
Negotiated with Charles of Anjou to take the Kingdom of Sicily
Never resided in Rome; died at Perugia on 2 October 1264

faqs.question: Did Pope Urban IV create the Feast of Corpus Christi?
faqs.answer: He made it a feast of the whole Church in 1264 with the bull Transiturus. The feast had begun earlier in the diocese of Liège, inspired by St. Juliana of Cornillon, where Urban had once served as archdeacon.

faqs.question: Did St. Thomas Aquinas write the Corpus Christi hymns for Urban IV?
faqs.answer: Tradition attributes the office of Corpus Christi, including Pange lingua and Tantum ergo, to Thomas Aquinas at Urban's request while the papal court was at Orvieto. Most historians accept the attribution, though it has been debated.

faqs.question: Why was Urban IV elected even though he was not a cardinal?
faqs.answer: Only a handful of cardinals were alive in 1261, and after three months they could not agree on one of themselves. They turned to Jacques Pantaléon, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, who happened to be at the papal court.
